questions.question: Annapurna Finance Private Limited had its origin as a not - for - profit company called __________, an NGO that helped poor women in Odisha.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Peoples Forum**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Annapurna Finance Private Limited was initially established as a **not-for-profit organization** under the name **Peoples Forum** in 1990.
 
• **Peoples Forum** was an NGO based in Odisha, aiming to support and empower poor and marginalized communities, particularly women.
 
• The organization focused on **poverty alleviation** through livelihood generation, financial literacy, and microfinance initiatives.
 
• In 2009, it transitioned into a Non-Banking Financial Company-Microfinance Institution (NBFC-MFI) to expand its outreach and formalize its financial services.
 
• Annapurna Finance is now one of India’s largest MFIs, providing **micro-loans** to rural and semi-urban populations to promote financial inclusion.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Microfinance Institutions (MFIs):**

 
 
• MFIs provide small loans to individuals who lack access to traditional banking services, helping them build sustainable livelihoods.
 
• They play a critical role in promoting **financial inclusion**, especially in rural and underserved areas.
 
 
 
• **Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs):**
 
 
• NBFCs are financial institutions that offer banking services without meeting the legal definition of a bank.
 
• They are regulated by the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** and play a significant role in the Indian financial ecosystem.
 
 
 
• **Women Empowerment through Microfinance:**
 
 
• Microfinance initiatives by organizations like Annapurna Finance have enabled women to become financially independent and contribute to household income.
 
• These programs also promote entrepreneurship and skill development among women.
 
 
 
• **Odisha's Socio-Economic Context:**
 
 
• Odisha has a significant rural population with limited access to formal financial systems.
 
• Organizations like Peoples Forum have played a key role in addressing poverty and improving living standards in the state.

questions.question: Hanukkah is a ______ festival.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Jewish**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Hanukkah, also known as the **Festival of Lights**, is a Jewish holiday celebrated for eight days and nights.
 
• It commemorates the rededication of the Second Temple in Jerusalem during the second century BCE after its desecration by the Seleucids.
 
• The holiday is observed by lighting the menorah (a nine-branched candelabrum), with one additional candle lit each night.
 
• Traditional foods such as latkes (potato pancakes) and sufganiyot (jelly-filled doughnuts) are consumed, symbolizing the miracle of the oil that burned for eight days.
 
• Hanukkah typically falls in November or December, according to the Jewish lunar calendar.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Menorah:** The menorah is a central symbol of Hanukkah, consisting of eight branches for the eight days of Hanukkah and one additional branch for the shamash (helper candle).
 
• **Miracle of the Oil:** According to Jewish tradition, a small amount of oil sufficient for one day miraculously burned for eight days during the rededication of the Second Temple.
 
• **Dreidel:** A traditional four-sided spinning top used during Hanukkah, with Hebrew letters symbolizing the phrase "A great miracle happened there."
 
• **Historical Context:** Hanukkah commemorates the victory of the Maccabees, a group of Jewish rebels, over the Seleucid Empire and the subsequent restoration of Jewish worship in the temple.
 
• **Significance:** Hanukkah is a celebration of religious freedom, resilience, and the perseverance of Jewish identity and traditions.

questions.question: In which year did Mihir Sen create history by being the only man to swim the five oceans in one calendar year?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1966**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Mihir Sen, an Indian long-distance swimmer, became the first man to swim across the five major oceans within one calendar year in **1966**.
 
• He successfully swam the Palk Strait (India-Sri Lanka), the Strait of Gibraltar (Europe-Africa), the Dardanelles (Turkey), the Bosporus (Turkey), and the Panama Canal (Central America) during this remarkable feat.
 
• This achievement established Mihir Sen as one of the world's most accomplished open-water swimmers and brought global recognition to Indian swimming.
 
• He became the only person to achieve this extraordinary accomplishment in a single calendar year, demonstrating tremendous endurance and resilience.
 
• Mihir Sen was awarded the Padma Shri and Padma Bhushan by the Indian government for his outstanding contributions to sports.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Open-water swimming:** This is a type of swimming conducted in outdoor bodies of water, such as oceans, lakes, and rivers, and requires exceptional physical stamina and mental strength.
 
• **Palk Strait:** A strait between Tamil Nadu in India and the Jaffna District of Sri Lanka, known for its challenging currents and shallow waters.
 
• **Strait of Gibraltar:** A narrow strait that connects the Atlantic Ocean to the Mediterranean Sea and separates Europe from Africa, known for its strong tidal currents.
 
• **Panama Canal:** An artificial waterway in Panama that connects the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans, presenting unique challenges for swimmers due to its controlled locks and currents.
 
• Mihir Sen's achievements are often compared to those of global swimming legends, making him a pioneer in Indian sports and a source of inspiration for athletes worldwide.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Meningitis is primarily transmitted via **droplet infection**, which involves the inhalation of respiratory droplets containing the pathogen. (a - iv)
 
• Rabies is transmitted through **inoculation into the skin or mucosa**, often via bites or scratches from infected animals. (b - i)
 
• Typhoid is caused by the ingestion of **contaminated food or water** containing the bacteria *Salmonella typhi*. (c - ii)
 
• Tetanus is contracted through **contact with soil** contaminated with *Clostridium tetani*, usually entering through wounds or cuts. (d - iii)

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Meningitis:**

 
 
• Meningitis is the inflammation of the membranes surrounding the brain and spinal cord.
 
• Caused by bacteria, viruses, fungi, or other pathogens; bacterial meningitis is the most severe form.
 
• Symptoms include fever, headache, stiff neck, and sensitivity to light.
 
 
 
• **Rabies:**
 
 
• Rabies is a viral disease causing severe encephalitis and is almost always fatal once symptoms appear.
 
• Vaccination post-exposure is essential to prevent disease progression.
 
• Dogs are the primary reservoir in most regions, but other animals like bats can also transmit rabies.
 
 
 
• **Typhoid:**
 
 
• Typhoid fever is caused by the bacterium *Salmonella typhi*.
 
• It spreads through ingestion of food or water contaminated by feces from infected individuals.
 
• Common symptoms include high fever, abdominal pain, and constipation or diarrhea.
 
 
 
• **Tetanus:**
 
 
• Tetanus is caused by a neurotoxin produced by the bacterium *Clostridium tetani*.
 
• It leads to muscle stiffness and spasms, commonly known as "lockjaw."
 
• Vaccination is the primary preventive measure against tetanus.

questions.question: Which edition of the FIFA U - 17 Women’s World Cup was hosted by India in 2022 ?

questions.question: According to Planning commission of India (2011 - 12), which group of states has the highest poverty ratio?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• As per the Planning Commission of India (2011-12), Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand recorded the **highest poverty ratio** among Indian states.
 
• The poverty ratio in Chhattisgarh was approximately **39.93%**, the highest in the country during the stated period.
 
• Jharkhand followed closely with a poverty ratio of around **37.0%**, placing it among the poorest states in India.
 
• Both states face challenges due to **economic underdevelopment, lack of industrialization, and poor access to social infrastructure**.
 
• The high poverty rates are attributed to issues like **low agricultural productivity, unemployment, and inadequate healthcare and education facilities**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Poverty Ratio Definition:** Poverty ratio refers to the proportion of the population living below the poverty line, which is defined based on income or consumption levels required for basic needs.
 
• **Planning Commission's Role:** The Planning Commission of India was responsible for assessing poverty levels in the country until it was replaced by NITI Aayog in 2015.
 
• **Poverty Line Measurement:** For 2011-12, poverty estimates were based on the Tendulkar methodology, which considers expenditure on food, education, and healthcare.
 
• **State-wise Challenges:** Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand are states with a significant tribal population, and their poverty rates are worsened by **lack of infrastructure, limited employment opportunities, and inadequate governance**.
 
• **Efforts to Address Poverty:** Government initiatives like MGNREGA (Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act) and NFSA (National Food Security Act) aim to alleviate poverty and improve living standards in these states.

questions.question: The Ramakrishna Mission was founded by _________ to regenerate Indian society by promoting the Vedanta philosophy.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Swami Vivekananda**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Swami Vivekananda** founded the Ramakrishna Mission in **1897** to spread the teachings of Vedanta and work towards the betterment of society.
 
• The organization was named after his guru, **Ramakrishna Paramahamsa**, whose spiritual teachings inspired Vivekananda.
 
• The mission focuses on the spiritual and social upliftment of humanity, emphasizing the harmony of religions and selfless service.
 
• The headquarters of the Ramakrishna Mission is located at **Belur Math**, in Howrah, West Bengal, India.
 
• It operates in the areas of education, health care, disaster relief, rural development, and cultural promotion.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Vedanta Philosophy**:

 
 
• Vedanta is a spiritual philosophy derived from the Upanishads, emphasizing the unity of all existence and the divinity of the soul.
 
• It teaches that the ultimate goal of life is self-realization and liberation (moksha).
 
 
 
• **Swami Vivekananda's Role**:
 
 
• He is widely recognized for his speech at the **World's Parliament of Religions in Chicago in 1893**, where he introduced Hindu philosophy to the West.
 
• He stressed the importance of service to humanity as a form of worship.
 
 
 
• **Ramakrishna Paramahamsa**:
 
 
• He was a 19th-century Indian mystic and spiritual teacher who emphasized the unity of all religions.
 
• His teachings greatly influenced Swami Vivekananda and formed the philosophical foundation for the Ramakrishna Mission.
 
 
 
• **Belur Math**:
 
 
• Belur Math serves as the global headquarters of the Ramakrishna Math and Mission.
 
• The architecture of Belur Math symbolizes religious harmony, blending Hindu, Christian, and Islamic motifs.
 
 
 
• **Ramakrishna Mission's Activities**:
 
 
• The mission is involved in providing free education, medical services, disaster relief, and promoting interfaith harmony.
 
• It also runs several schools, colleges, and hospitals across India and abroad.

questions.question: ‘Koman’ and ‘Kuruwa’ are the names of _________ in India.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**slash and burn agriculture**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **'Koman'** and **'Kuruwa'** are traditional terms used to describe forms of slash and burn agriculture in India.
 
• Slash and burn agriculture is referred to as **'Jhum' cultivation** in northeastern states like Assam, Nagaland, and Meghalaya.
 
• In Odisha and Jharkhand, this practice is often called **'Koman'** and **'Kuruwa'**, respectively.
 
• It involves cutting and burning forests or vegetation to create fields for cultivation, usually practiced by tribal communities in hilly or forested regions.
 
• This method is widely used for subsistence farming but has significant environmental implications, including deforestation and soil degradation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Slash and Burn Agriculture**:

 
 
• This is a traditional agricultural practice where natural vegetation is cleared by cutting and burning to prepare the land for farming.
 
• It is a form of shifting cultivation, where fields are cultivated temporarily and then abandoned for natural regeneration.
 
 
 
• **Environmental Impacts**:
 
 
• Deforestation and loss of biodiversity.
 
• Soil erosion and depletion of soil fertility due to frequent burning and lack of crop rotation.
 
 
 
• **Regional Names in India**:
 
 
• 'Jhum' in the northeastern states.
 
• 'Podu' in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana.
 
• 'Bewar' or 'Dahiya' in Madhya Pradesh.
 
 
 
• **Government Initiatives**:
 
 
• Programs promoting sustainable agriculture and afforestation to reduce the harmful effects of slash and burn practices.
 
• Encouragement of settled farming through irrigation and soil conservation programs.

questions.question: In which of the following sessions did the Indian National Congress decide to boycott the Simon Commission?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Madras session**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Indian National Congress decided to boycott the Simon Commission during the **Madras session held in 1927**.
 
• The Simon Commission, appointed in 1927 by the British government, faced opposition as it **lacked any Indian representation**.
 
• The boycott of the Simon Commission was a significant step in India's freedom movement as it demonstrated **unified resistance to colonial policies.**
 
• During the Madras session, leaders like **Motilal Nehru and Jawaharlal Nehru** played pivotal roles in advocating for the boycott.
 
• The slogan "**Simon Go Back**" became a rallying cry for Indians, showcasing widespread discontent with British rule.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Simon Commission:**

 
 
• It was constituted in 1927 to review the working of the Government of India Act, 1919, and suggest constitutional reforms.
 
• The absence of Indian members in the commission led to massive protests and its rejection by Indian leaders.
 
 
 
• **Madras Session of 1927:**
 
 
• It was a landmark session of the Indian National Congress presided over by **Dr. M.A. Ansari**.
 
• The decision to boycott the Simon Commission was one of the key resolutions passed during this session.
 
 
 
• **Impact of the Boycott:**
 
 
• The boycott strengthened the resolve for greater autonomy and eventually complete independence from British rule.
 
• It also led to the drafting of the **Nehru Report (1928)**, which proposed a dominion status constitution for India.
 
 
 
• **Slogan “Simon Go Back”:**
 
 
• It symbolized the unity of Indians across all regions and communities against British colonial policies.
 
• Prominent leaders like Lala Lajpat Rai opposed the commission, and his death due to police brutality during protests further intensified the resistance.

questions.question: In 1991, India met with an economic crisis where the _________ reserves fell so low that they were not sufficient for even a _________ .
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**foreign exchange; fortnight**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• In 1991, India faced a severe economic crisis characterized by a **sharp decline in foreign exchange reserves**.
 
• The **foreign exchange reserves** fell to such a low level that they were insufficient to cover **imports for even two weeks (a fortnight).**
 
• The crisis was primarily caused by a **high fiscal deficit, rising inflation, and external debt accumulation.**
 
• India was on the verge of **defaulting on its external obligations**, forcing the government to pledge its gold reserves as collateral for loans.
 
• This crisis led to the initiation of **economic liberalization reforms in 1991** under the leadership of Prime Minister P.V. Narasimha Rao and Finance Minister Dr. Manmohan Singh.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Foreign Exchange Reserves**

 
 
• Foreign exchange reserves are assets held by a country’s central bank in foreign currencies, used to back liabilities and influence monetary policy.
 
• India's reserves include foreign currency assets, gold, Special Drawing Rights (SDRs), and reserve positions in the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
 
 
 
• **Economic Liberalization in India**
 
 
• The 1991 reforms focused on **deregulation, privatization, and opening up the economy to foreign investment.**
 
• Key measures included reducing import tariffs, allowing foreign direct investment (FDI), and dismantling the License Raj.
 
 
 
• **Balance of Payments Crisis**
 
 
• The Balance of Payments (BoP) crisis refers to a situation where a country is unable to meet its international payment obligations due to insufficient foreign exchange reserves.
 
• India’s 1991 BoP crisis was caused by **high oil prices, reduced remittances, and a global slowdown.**
 
 
 
• **Gold Pledging in 1991**
 
 
• To avoid default, India pledged **67 tons of gold** to the Bank of England and Union Bank of Switzerland.
 
• This move was a temporary measure to secure loans and stabilize the economy.

questions.question: Kailasa temple is made up of which of the following types of rock?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Basalt**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Kailasa temple, part of the Ellora Caves in Maharashtra, India, is carved from a single massive block of **Basalt rock**.
 
• It is a monolithic rock-cut structure, meaning it was entirely excavated from a single rock formation.
 
• The temple was commissioned during the reign of the Rashtrakuta king **Krishna I** in the 8th century CE.
 
• Basalt, a volcanic igneous rock, was chosen due to its durability and relatively easier carving properties compared to other rocks like granite.
 
• The temple is considered an architectural marvel and a UNESCO World Heritage Site, renowned for its intricate carvings and massive scale.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Basalt Rock:**

 
 
• Basalt is an extrusive igneous rock formed by the rapid cooling of basaltic lava near the Earth's surface.
 
• It is composed mainly of minerals like plagioclase and pyroxene, making it dense and hard.
 
• Due to its abundance and properties, basalt has been historically used in construction and sculpture.
 
 
 
• **Ellora Caves:**
 
 
• The Ellora Caves comprise 34 rock-cut monasteries and temples, representing Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain traditions.
 
• The Kailasa temple (Cave 16) is the largest and most famous structure in the complex.
 
 
 
• **Monolithic Architecture:**
 
 
• Monolithic structures are carved from a single rock, requiring immense planning and precision.
 
• The Kailasa temple is a prime example, showcasing advanced engineering and artistic skills of ancient India.
 
 
 
• **Rashtrakuta Dynasty:**
 
 
• The Rashtrakutas were a prominent Indian dynasty during the 8th–10th centuries CE.
 
• They are credited with commissioning several architectural wonders, including the Kailasa temple.

questions.question: Suppose a person has four acres of land in India, and he actually needs only two workers and himself to carry out various operations on his farm in a year, but if he employs five workers and his family members such as his wife and children”, this situation known as ____________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Disguised Unemployment**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Disguised Unemployment** occurs when more people are employed in a task than are actually required, leading to reduced productivity per worker.
 
• In the given scenario, only two workers and the person are needed for the farm operations, but five additional workers and family members are employed, showcasing disguised unemployment.
 
• This type of unemployment is prevalent in rural areas, especially in the **agriculture sector of India**, where land and resources are limited.
 
• It is a form of underemployment where workers appear to be employed but their contribution to output is negligible or zero.
 
• It often reflects inefficiencies in resource allocation and is a sign of economic underdevelopment.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Types of Unemployment:**

 
 
• **Open Unemployment:** Refers to individuals who are willing to work but cannot find jobs.
 
• **Seasonal Unemployment:** Occurs when people are unemployed during certain seasons, common in the agricultural sector.
 
• **Transitional Unemployment:** Happens when individuals are in between jobs or transitioning from one job to another.
 
 
 
• **Features of Disguised Unemployment:**
 
 
• Common in developing countries with a large agricultural workforce.
 
• Resources like land and capital remain underutilized due to surplus labor.
 
• Does not contribute to increased output or productivity despite additional workers.
 
 
 
• **Implications of Disguised Unemployment:**
 
 
• Leads to low-income levels and poor living standards in rural areas.
 
• Indicates inefficient labor allocation and lack of industrial or non-agricultural job opportunities.
 
 
 
• **Measures to Address Disguised Unemployment:**
 
 
• Promoting industrialization and creating non-agricultural jobs.
 
• Improving agricultural productivity through modernization and technological advancements.
 
• Encouraging skill development and vocational training programs.

questions.question: The horizontal distance between two adjacent crests or troughs is known as the __________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**wave length**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The horizontal distance between two adjacent crests or troughs in a wave is referred to as the **wavelength**.
 
• It is denoted by the Greek letter **λ (lambda)** and is typically measured in units such as meters (m), centimeters (cm), or nanometers (nm).
 
• Wavelength is a fundamental property of waves, including light waves, sound waves, and water waves.
 
• It is inversely related to the wave's frequency: **wavelength = wave speed / frequency**.
 
• Longer wavelengths correspond to lower frequencies, while shorter wavelengths correspond to higher frequencies.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Wave Frequency:**

 
 
• Frequency refers to the number of wave cycles that pass a given point per second.
 
• It is measured in **Hertz (Hz)**, where 1 Hz equals one cycle per second.
 
• The relationship between frequency and wavelength is inverse: as frequency increases, wavelength decreases.
 
 
 
• **Wave Period:**
 
 
• The wave period is the time it takes for one complete wave cycle to pass a point.
 
• It is the reciprocal of frequency: **Period = 1 / Frequency**.
 
 
 
• **Wave Speed:**
 
 
• The speed at which a wave propagates through a medium is called wave speed.
 
• It can be calculated using the formula: **Wave speed = Wavelength × Frequency**.
 
 
 
• **Crests and Troughs:**
 
 
• A crest is the highest point of a wave, while a trough is the lowest point.
 
• The distance between two consecutive crests or troughs is the wavelength.
 
 
 
• **Types of Waves:**

questions.question: Fundamental duties were first added by which Constitutional Amendment Act ?

• The Fundamental Duties were introduced to the Indian Constitution by the **42nd Constitutional Amendment Act in 1976**.
 
• This amendment added **Article 51A** under Part IVA of the Constitution, listing the Fundamental Duties of citizens.
 
• It was implemented during the tenure of Prime Minister **Indira Gandhi** as part of the recommendations of the Swaran Singh Committee.
 
• Initially, **10 Fundamental Duties** were listed, which were later increased to 11 by the **86th Constitutional Amendment Act in 2002**.
 
• The objective of Fundamental Duties is to remind citizens of their moral obligations towards the nation and promote a sense of discipline and commitment.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• It amended various aspects, including the Preamble, Fundamental Rights, and Directive Principles of State Policy.
 
• Introduced terms like "Socialist" and "Secular" in the Preamble to emphasize India's commitment to these principles.
 
• Strengthened the central government by curbing the powers of the state governments.
 
 
 
• **Fundamental Duties:**
 
 
• Inspired by the Constitution of the Soviet Union, they aim to inculcate civic responsibility among citizens.

• Unlike Fundamental Rights, Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable, meaning they cannot be enforced through courts.

questions.question: In an economy, if the gross national product at factor cost is ₹10,000 crores, depreciation is ₹250 crores, the net factor income from abroad is ₹500 crores, what is the value of national income ?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**₹9,750 crores**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Gross National Product (GNP) at factor cost is the market value of goods and services produced by a country's residents, including income from abroad, minus production costs.
 
• The formula for national income (Net National Product at factor cost) is: **National Income = GNP at factor cost - Depreciation**.
 
• In the given problem, GNP at factor cost = ₹10,000 crores, and depreciation = ₹250 crores.
 
• National Income = ₹10,000 crores - ₹250 crores = ₹9,750 crores.
 
• Depreciation represents the reduction in the value of capital assets due to wear and tear over time.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Gross National Product (GNP):** Measures the total economic output produced by a country’s residents, including income from abroad.
 
• **Net National Product (NNP):** Derived by subtracting depreciation from the GNP. It represents the actual income available to the country.
 
• **Depreciation:** Also referred to as capital consumption, it accounts for the loss in value of fixed assets over time due to usage.
 
• **Net Factor Income from Abroad:** Refers to the difference between income earned by domestic residents abroad and income earned by foreign residents domestically.
 
• In economic terms, **National Income** reflects the sum of the incomes earned by residents of a country, minus depreciation, and is a key indicator of economic health.

questions.question: On which of the following matters of the State List can Delhi’s Legislature make laws?

__
 
• The Delhi Legislative Assembly is empowered to make laws on subjects in the **State List and Concurrent List** except for matters explicitly excluded under the Constitution.
 
• Subjects such as **Police, Public Order, and Land** are excluded from the purview of Delhi's Legislature as per Article 239AA of the Indian Constitution.
 
• Health is a subject in the **State List** on which Delhi's Legislature can formulate laws, as it is not included in the excluded matters.
 
• The National Capital Territory of Delhi operates under a unique governance structure, with limited autonomy compared to full-fledged states.
 
• The Lieutenant Governor of Delhi plays a significant role in matters concerning law-making by the Delhi Legislative Assembly, particularly for reserved subjects.

• **Article 239AA:** Introduced by the 69th Constitutional Amendment Act, it provides a special status to Delhi as the National Capital Territory (NCT) with a Legislative Assembly.
 
• **State List:** This list enumerates subjects on which states can legislate, including health, agriculture, and local governance, among others.
 
• **Union Territories Act, 1991:** This Act governs the administration of the NCT of Delhi, delineating the roles of the Legislative Assembly and the Lieutenant Governor.
 
• **Concurrent List:** Subjects in this list can be legislated upon by both the Parliament and State Legislatures, with Parliament's law prevailing in case of conflict.
 
• **Governance in Delhi:** Unlike other states, Delhi's governance is shared between the **Delhi Government** and the **Central Government**, with the latter having significant control over excluded subjects.

questions.question: Which of the following is the function of trade barriers?

options.text: Restrict the flow of international goods and services
Restrict the flow of Indian goods and services in India

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Restrict the flow of international goods and services**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Trade barriers are measures implemented by governments to control the flow of goods and services across international borders, often to protect domestic industries.
 
• These barriers include tariffs (taxes on imports), quotas (limits on the number of goods that can be imported), and non-tariff barriers like licensing and standards.
 
• The primary purpose of trade barriers is to **restrict international competition** and encourage the growth of local industries by limiting the availability of foreign products.
 
• They can also be used to safeguard national security, protect jobs, or enforce trade sanctions against specific countries.
 
• While trade barriers can benefit domestic producers, they may also lead to higher prices for consumers and trade tensions between countries.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Types of Trade Barriers:**

 
 
• **Tariffs:** Taxes imposed on imported goods to make them more expensive than domestic products.
 
• **Quotas:** Numerical limits on the quantity of goods that can be imported.
 
• **Subsidies:** Financial support provided to domestic industries to make them more competitive against foreign imports.
 
• **Non-tariff barriers:** Regulations or standards that make it harder for foreign goods to enter the market, such as health and safety standards.
 
 
 
• **Impact of Trade Barriers:**
 
 
• Positive: Protects local industries and jobs, encourages domestic production, and enhances national security.
 
• Negative: Increases prices for consumers, limits product variety, and can lead to retaliatory measures by other countries.
 
 
 
• **Examples of Trade Barriers:**
 
 
• The Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act of 1930 imposed high tariffs on imports into the U.S., worsening the global economic depression.
 
• The EU imposes quotas on certain agricultural products to protect its farmers.
 
 
 
• **Global Trade Organizations:**
 
 
• **World Trade Organization (WTO):** Works to reduce trade barriers globally and resolve trade disputes between nations.
 
• **Regional Trade Agreements:** Examples include NAFTA (now USMCA) and the European Union, which aim to reduce barriers within specific regions.
 
 
 
• **Recent Trends:** Many countries are revisiting trade barriers to protect local industries amidst global economic shifts, as seen during the COVID-19 pandemic and ongoing geopolitical tensions.

questions.question: Which of the following is known as the power house of cells?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Mitochondria**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Mitochondria** are membrane-bound organelles found in most eukaryotic cells and are often referred to as the "powerhouse of the cell."
 
• They generate **adenosine triphosphate (ATP)**, the primary energy currency of the cell, through the process of cellular respiration.
 
• Mitochondria have a double-membrane structure, with the inner membrane being highly folded into structures called **cristae**, which maximize the surface area for energy production.
 
• They play a key role not only in energy production but also in **regulating cellular metabolism**, calcium storage, and apoptosis (programmed cell death).
 
• Mitochondria have their own **DNA and ribosomes**, allowing them to produce some of their own proteins independently of the cell nucleus.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Cellular Respiration:**

 
 
• This is the process by which mitochondria produce ATP. It involves three main stages: glycolysis, the citric acid cycle (Krebs cycle), and oxidative phosphorylation.
 
• Oxygen is essential for the electron transport chain in oxidative phosphorylation, which produces the majority of ATP.
 
 
 
• **Endosymbiotic Theory:**
 
 
• The theory suggests that mitochondria originated from free-living prokaryotic cells that were engulfed by ancestral eukaryotic cells.
 
• Evidence for this includes the presence of mitochondrial DNA and the double-membrane structure.
 
 
 
• **Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA):**
 
 
• Mitochondria contain their own circular DNA, which is inherited maternally in most organisms.
 
• Mutations in mtDNA can lead to mitochondrial diseases, which often affect energy-demanding organs like the brain, heart, and muscles.
 
 
 
• **Apoptosis:**
 
 
• Mitochondria play a central role in apoptosis by releasing cytochrome c, which activates a cascade of proteins called caspases that lead to cell death.
 
• This process is crucial for maintaining tissue homeostasis and removing damaged or unwanted cells.
 
 
 
• **Other Functions:**
 
 
• Besides energy production, mitochondria are involved in heat generation (thermogenesis) in brown adipose tissue.
 
• They also contribute to the synthesis of certain steroids and heme, a component of hemoglobin.

questions.question: In the context of globalisation, FDI is an important term. What does the I stand for in FDI?
questions.solution:

__
 
• **FDI** stands for **Foreign Direct Investment**, where the "I" refers to Investment__.
 
• It involves an individual or a business entity from one country making a **direct investment** into a business or entity located in another country.
 
• FDI is a crucial indicator of economic globalization, as it reflects the movement of capital across borders for productive purposes.
 
• It is different from portfolio investments, which involve the **purchase of stocks or bonds** without direct control over the business operations.
 
• FDI can take two primary forms: **greenfield investments** (creating new facilities) and **mergers/acquisitions** (buying existing assets).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Greenfield Investment:** A type of FDI where a company establishes new operations or facilities from the ground up in a foreign country.
 
• **Brownfield Investment:** Involves the purchase or lease of existing production facilities to launch a new production activity.
 
• **FDI Benefits:** Includes increased employment, access to advanced technology, and boosting the host country's economic development.
 
• **Host and Home Country:** The host country__ is where the investment is made, while the __home country__ is where the investor is based.
 
• **FDI Trends:** Developed countries like the USA and developing economies like India are significant recipients of FDI due to their market potential, policy reforms, and infrastructure.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about water resource is correct?

options.text: Water is a non - renewable resource.
Water is both, biotic and abiotic resource.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Water is a cyclic resource.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Water is a cyclic resource** as it continuously moves through the hydrological cycle, including processes like evaporation, condensation, precipitation, and infiltration.
 
• The water cycle ensures that water is replenished naturally through natural processes, making it a renewable resource.
 
• Despite being renewable, water availability depends on factors like geography, climate, and human usage, which can lead to shortages in certain areas.
 
• Water is classified as an **abiotic resource** because it is non-living and forms a part of the Earth's physical environment.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Hydrological Cycle:** The continuous movement of water on, above, and below the Earth's surface. It includes processes such as evaporation (water turning into vapor), condensation (vapor turning into liquid), and precipitation (rain, snow, etc.).
 
• **Renewable Resource:** Water is considered renewable because it is naturally replenished through the water cycle. However, misuse or overexploitation can lead to water scarcity.
 
• **Abiotic Resource:** These are non-living resources, such as water, air, soil, and minerals, that support life and ecosystems.
 
• **Water Scarcity:** A condition where water demand exceeds supply due to factors like overpopulation, pollution, and climate change. Sustainable water management is essential to avoid scarcity.
 
• **Global Distribution:** About 71% of the Earth’s surface is covered by water, but only 2.5% of it is freshwater. Of this, a significant portion is locked in glaciers and ice caps, leaving less than 1% accessible for human use.

questions.question: Irregular growth of teeth is due to the deficiencies of vitamin ____.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Vitamin D**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Vitamin D** plays a crucial role in calcium absorption and bone health, which is essential for proper dental growth and alignment.
 
• Deficiency of Vitamin D can lead to improper mineralization of teeth, causing irregular growth and dental deformities.
 
• Conditions such as **rickets** (in children) and **osteomalacia** (in adults) due to Vitamin D deficiency can affect jawbone development and tooth alignment.
 
• Sources of Vitamin D include exposure to sunlight, fortified foods, fatty fish, and dietary supplements.
 
• Proper intake of Vitamin D is especially important during childhood, as it is a critical period for dental and skeletal development.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Rickets:** A condition caused by Vitamin D deficiency in children leading to weak or soft bones, dental issues, and skeletal deformities.
 
• **Osteomalacia:** Softening of bones in adults due to poor bone mineralization, often linked with Vitamin D deficiency.
 
• **Calcium and Vitamin D:** Both nutrients work in synergy; Vitamin D enhances calcium absorption in the intestines, necessary for strong teeth and bones.
 
• **Hypervitaminosis D:** Excessive Vitamin D intake can lead to toxicity, causing hypercalcemia (high calcium levels) and affecting overall health.
 
• **Sunlight Exposure:** The body synthesizes Vitamin D naturally when skin is exposed to sunlight; however, factors like pollution, sunscreen, and lifestyle can limit this process.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Rashtrakuta ruler Dantidurga was succeeded by his uncle **Krishna I** after he died without a male heir.
 
• Krishna I is credited with consolidating the Rashtrakuta empire and expanding its territories.
 
• He was a great patron of art and architecture, most notably associated with the construction of the **Kailasa Temple at Ellora**.
 
• Krishna I ruled during the late 8th century CE and played a key role in strengthening the Rashtrakuta dynasty.
 
• He defeated the Ganga dynasty and other rivals, ensuring Rashtrakuta supremacy in peninsular India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Rashtrakuta Dynasty:**

 
 
• The Rashtrakutas were a prominent dynasty in southern and central India between the 6th and 10th centuries CE.
 
• Their empire extended from the Vindhyas in the north to Kanyakumari in the south.
 
• They are well-known for their contributions to art, literature, and architecture.
 
 
 
• **Kailasa Temple:**
 
 
• Constructed under the patronage of Krishna I, the Kailasa Temple is a rock-cut monolithic structure at Ellora.
 
• The temple is dedicated to Lord Shiva and is considered an architectural marvel of ancient India.
 
• It showcases intricate carvings and sculptures that depict various Hindu mythological themes.
 
 
 
• **Dantidurga:**
 
 
• Also known as Dantivarman, he was the founder of the Rashtrakuta dynasty.
 
• He overthrew the Chalukyas of Badami to establish Rashtrakuta dominance in the Deccan region.
 
• His reign marked the beginning of a powerful lineage that influenced Indian history.
 
 
 
• **Ellora Caves:**
 
 
• A UNESCO World Heritage site, the Ellora Caves are located in Maharashtra, India.
 
• The site consists of 34 rock-cut monasteries and temples belonging to Buddhist, Hindu, and Jain traditions.
 
• The Kailasa Temple (Cave 16) is the most famous structure within this complex.

questions.question: Which famous chemist refuted the theory of 'vitalism' by saying that organic substances can only be produced from living things?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Friedrich Wohler**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Friedrich Wohler** was a German chemist who is best known for his synthesis of urea in 1828, which disproved the theory of vitalism.
 
• The theory of vitalism proposed that organic compounds could only be produced by living organisms, as they required a "vital force."
 
• Wohler synthesized urea, an organic compound, from inorganic ammonium cyanate, proving that organic substances can be created in a lab setting.
 
• This breakthrough is considered a foundational moment in organic chemistry and marked the beginning of modern chemical synthesis of organic compounds.
 
• His work demonstrated that the chemical processes in living organisms obey the same natural laws as those outside of them.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Vitalism:** A discredited scientific theory suggesting that living organisms possess a "vital force" that is absent in non-living matter, making their chemistry unique.
 
• **Urea:** A nitrogen-containing compound that is a major component of urine in mammals; Wohler's synthesis of urea was a key step in the development of organic chemistry.
 
• **Ammonium Cyanate:** The inorganic compound used by Wohler to synthesize urea; it demonstrated the transformation of inorganic to organic compounds.
 
• **Impact of Wohler's Discovery:** This experiment laid the groundwork for debunking the separation between organic and inorganic chemistry, unifying the field of chemistry as a whole.
 
• **Modern Organic Chemistry:** Wohler's work paved the way for the artificial synthesis of numerous organic compounds, including drugs, plastics, and dyes, revolutionizing industries worldwide.

questions.question: With which of the following states is the ‘Popir’ dance associated ?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Arunachal Pradesh**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Popir** is a traditional dance form associated with the state of **Arunachal Pradesh**.
 
• The dance is performed by the **Adi tribe**, one of the major tribes of Arunachal Pradesh.
 
• Popir is typically performed during **festivals and celebrations**, such as the Solung Festival, which is celebrated to mark prosperity and agricultural success.
 
• The dance involves vibrant costumes, rhythmic movements, and songs, which reflect the **cultural richness** of the Adi tribe.
 
• It is an important cultural tradition and plays a vital role in preserving the heritage of the **indigenous communities of Arunachal Pradesh**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Adi Tribe:**

 
 
• The Adi tribe is one of the largest ethnic groups in Arunachal Pradesh.
 
• They mainly inhabit the districts of East Siang, Upper Siang, and West Siang.
 
• Their traditional festivals, such as Solung and Aran, revolve around agriculture and community welfare.
 
 
 
• **Solung Festival:**
 
 
• Solung is a major agricultural festival celebrated by the Adi tribe.
 
• It is observed in the month of September and signifies prayers for prosperity and a good harvest.
 
• Popir dance is a central feature of the festival celebrations.
 
 
 
• **Traditional Dance in India:**
 
 
• India has a rich tradition of folk and tribal dances, each reflecting the unique cultural heritage of different states and communities.
 
• Other notable tribal dances include Bihu (Assam), Ghoomar (Rajasthan), and Dhamail (Tripura).
 
 
 
• **Preservation of Culture:**
 
 
• Efforts are being made by the government and cultural organizations to preserve and promote tribal art and dance forms like Popir.
 
• Such initiatives help sustain the cultural identity of indigenous communities.

questions.question: The first Battle of Panipat was fought on 20 April 1526 between Babur and _______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Ibrahim Lodi**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The first Battle of Panipat was fought on **20 April 1526**, marking the beginning of the Mughal Empire in India.
 
• It was fought between **Babur**, the founder of the Mughal Empire, and **Ibrahim Lodi**, the last ruler of the Delhi Sultanate.
 
• Babur’s forces utilized the **"Tulughma" strategy** (division of forces into flanking and central units) and advanced artillery, which gave them a decisive advantage.
 
• Ibrahim Lodi commanded an army of approximately **100,000 soldiers and 1,000 war elephants**, but Babur's smaller, disciplined army of around 12,000 soldiers outmaneuvered and defeated him.
 
• The battle resulted in the death of Ibrahim Lodi and the establishment of Mughal rule in northern India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Babur**: A descendant of Timur and Genghis Khan, Babur was the founder of the Mughal Empire in India. His use of advanced artillery in the Battle of Panipat was revolutionary.
 
• **Ibrahim Lodi**: The last ruler of the Lodi dynasty, he faced internal dissent and lacked the military innovations required to counter Babur's forces effectively.
 
• **Tulughma Strategy**: This strategy involved dividing the army into left, right, and center units to encircle and overwhelm the enemy. Babur used this tactic effectively against Ibrahim Lodi.
 
• **Artillery**: Babur's use of field artillery, brought to India with the help of Ottoman expert Ustad Ali Quli, played a key role in his victory.
 
• **Significance of the Battle**: The first Battle of Panipat marked the end of the Delhi Sultanate and the beginning of Mughal dominance, which lasted for over three centuries.

questions.question: Who among the following has the power to make provision as he/she may think fit for the discharge of the functions of the Governor of a State in any contingency?

options.text: Chief Justice of the High Court

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**President**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The President of India has the authority to make provisions for the discharge of the functions of the Governor of a State in any contingency under **Article 160 of the Indian Constitution**.
 
• If a Governor is unable to perform their duties due to absence, illness, or any other reason, the President can appoint a person to discharge the Governor's duties temporarily.
 
• This provision allows the central authority to ensure the proper functioning of the State Government without disruption in governance.
 
• The President’s decision in such situations is made in accordance with the advice of the **Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister**.
 
• The role of the President in such scenarios highlights the unitary features of the Indian Constitution, ensuring smooth state-level governance in emergencies.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Article 160 of the Indian Constitution**: This article empowers the President to make provisions as deemed necessary for handling contingencies related to the Governor’s role in a state.
 
• **Governor's Role:** The Governor acts as the constitutional head of a state, appointed by the President for a term of five years.
 
• **Unitary Bias of Indian Federalism:** Situations like these demonstrate the centralizing tendencies of Indian federalism where the President steps in to ensure governance continuity.
 
• **Council of Ministers:** The President acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister in executing such provisions.
 
• **Emergency Provisions:** Besides Article 160, other emergency provisions like President’s Rule (Article 356) also highlight the mechanisms for managing state-level administrative crises.

questions.question: From which Five - Year Plan period was the formulation and implementation of the Five - Year Plan discontinued by the Government of India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Twelfth Five - Year Plan**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Government of India discontinued the formulation of Five-Year Plans after the Twelfth Five-Year Plan (2012–2017).
 
• This decision marked a significant shift in the planning process, transitioning from centralized planning to a decentralized framework.
 
• The NITI Aayog (National Institution for Transforming India) replaced the Planning Commission in January 2015, signaling the end of the Five-Year Plan era.
 
• The Twelfth Five-Year Plan focused on "Faster, More Inclusive, and Sustainable Growth" but was the last of its kind as the government moved towards rolling plans and sector-specific strategies.
 
• The discontinuation reflected a modern approach to policy-making, emphasizing flexibility and real-time monitoring over rigid long-term plans.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Planning Commission:**

 
 
• Established in 1950, it was responsible for drafting Five-Year Plans based on India's economic priorities.
 
• It was replaced by the NITI Aayog in 2015 to promote a bottom-up approach to planning.
 
 
 
• **NITI Aayog:**
 
 
• Formed on January 1, 2015, it serves as a policy think tank for the Government of India.
 
• It focuses on cooperative federalism, involving states in the planning process.
 
 
 
• **Rolling Plans:**
 
 
• Introduced as a replacement for Five-Year Plans, they allow for flexibility and periodic adjustments based on real-time needs.
 
• These plans focus on sector-specific growth strategies rather than a fixed timeline.
 
 
 
• **History of Five-Year Plans in India:**
 
 
• The first Five-Year Plan was launched in 1951, focusing on agriculture and irrigation.
 
• A total of 12 plans were implemented, with priorities shifting to industry, infrastructure, and social sectors over time.
